clips.title: Temporal Live Coding Demo: Handling Failures & Human Interaction
clips.why: A live demo of a worker crash in the middle of a run and of an API that is down, and how retries bring both back without any code of your own.
look: The worker process is killed while the order is being processed. Watch where the run continues when a worker comes back.
When the API is down, the activity fails again and again, and the retry policy keeps trying until the API returns.
clips.after: Our deploys are the same crash on purpose: the orchestrator's worker dies, and Temporal gives the activity to a new worker.

clips.title: The 4 Types of Timeouts in Temporal
clips.why: Maxim Fateev, who co-created Temporal, explains why one long timeout is not enough for a long activity, and how the heartbeat timeout fixes it.
look: Start-to-close is the limit for one attempt. Ask yourself what a long activity needs here, and how slowly a crash would be noticed with only this timeout. He also compares it with schedule-to-close, a limit on all attempts together, which this lesson does not need.
The heartbeat timeout: a long activity reports often, so a lost worker is detected quickly however long the activity is allowed to run.
clips.after: This is exactly the LONG preset: 7 days for start-to-close because the SDK requires it, and a 2-minute heartbeat that does the real work.

practice.q: The worker following Nova's build dies at minute 20. The activity has startToCloseTimeout '7 days' and heartbeatTimeout '2 minutes'. When does Temporal start attempt 2?

options.text: About 2 minutes after the last heartbeat
options.why: The heartbeat timeout is the gap Temporal allows between heartbeats. After that, the attempt is ended and a new one is scheduled.

options.text: After 7 days, when the start-to-close timeout passes
options.why: That would be the case without a heartbeat timeout. The heartbeat notices the dead worker much sooner.

options.text: Right away, because Temporal sees the worker process exit
options.why: Temporal cannot see processes. It only notices that the heartbeats stopped.

practice.why: heartbeatDetails carries the last progress Temporal received, so attempt 2 can continue instead of starting at step 1.

practice.q: The orchestrator is deployed while Nova builds RH-1234. Put what happens in order.
items: workInSandbox (attempt 1) follows the harness and sends a heartbeat every 30 seconds
The deploy stops the old worker process, and its heartbeats stop
After 2 minutes without a heartbeat, Temporal ends attempt 1 and schedules attempt 2
A worker from the new deploy takes attempt 2 and finds the harness already running on the VM
Attempt 2 follows the same harness, and Nova finishes the build without noticing
practice.why: The heartbeat timeout notices the dead worker, and the check for a running harness turns the retry into a re-attach.

options.text: Posting the plan to the ticket's Slack thread
options.why: It takes a second or two. A 5-minute start-to-close timeout notices a problem soon enough.

options.text: Following the harness while Nova builds for an hour
options.why: It runs far longer than any sensible timeout, so only a heartbeat can tell a working attempt from a dead one.

options.text: Reading the ticket's description from Jira
options.why: A short call. If it hangs, the 5-minute timeout ends the attempt and the retry policy tries again.
